BUILT WITH RELATIONSHIP SCIENTISTS ● APPLICATIONS OPEN · COHORT 01
I HEREBY COMMIT

Science has been studying love with sophomores more in need of a psych credit than a life partner.¹ The online dating industry stops paying attention at the match. We're fixing both with a first-of-its-kind experiment designed with the best scientists in the field from day 1 — to get the right data, get you on the right dates, and get some answers about what makes a relationship last.

Apply to be part of our first-of-its-kind study on what makes a match last.

To do this we need to study both singles and couples, of all ages, so please implore your single and partnered friends to donate their data to this important cause! It will be fun, we promise (have you met our founder?). Applications are reviewed & prioritized in order.

WHAT YOU THINK SCIENCE KNOWS
MYTH
Couples last when they speak each other's love language.
There's little evidence love languages exist.²
People appreciate all five, and matching yours doesn't reliably make couples happier.
MYTH
Introverts belong with introverts. Or with extroverts.
It barely matters.³
Personality similarity explains less than half a percent of how satisfied married couples are — about a tenth of what your partner's actual personality explains.
MYTH
The right questionnaire can find your match.
Chemistry can't be predicted on paper.⁴
Given 100+ traits and preferences, machine learning could predict who's generally desirable — but not which two people would click.
MYTH
Love is stronger when everyone's against it.
Your friends are usually right.⁵
The Romeo and Juliet effect was retested with the original 1972 measures. Parental approval predicted more love and commitment four months later. Opposition predicted less.

So why do we ask what you're looking for? Because nobody has tested it where it counts. Joel, Eastwick & Finkel found stated preferences didn't predict attraction in four-minute speed dates.⁴ We're testing them on real introductions people applied for.

WHAT SCIENCE ACTUALLY KNOWS
Commitment is the second-strongest predictor of whether a relationship survives.⁶
Across 137 longitudinal studies and 37,761 people, only one factor outperformed it — and that one rests on five studies. Commitment rests on fifty-eight.
It's the most replicated finding in the field, and it's the one we're named after.

Apply to be part of our first-of-its-kind study on what makes a match last.

  1. Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010), Behavioral and Brain Sciences.
  2. Impett, Park & Muise (2024), Current Directions in Psychological Science.
  3. Dyrenforth, Kashy, Donnellan & Lucas (2010), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
  4. Joel, Eastwick & Finkel (2017), Psychological Science.
  5. Sinclair, Hood & Wright (2014), Social Psychology.
  6. Le, Dove, Agnew, Korn & Mutso (2010), Personal Relationships, 17, 377–390.

Why we ask
Why we ask

How we use your preferences: we use what you're looking for as a starting point for introductions, and we test whether those stated preferences actually predict who you click with. Research shows they often don't in speed dating; we're testing them on real introductions.

Private by defaultWe collect preferences to test whether they predict anything — not to match on them.
